How a negotiation becomes an agreement

Original motion graphics and synthetic narration. Fictional dialogue; educational reconstruction, not an official WHO film. Reviewed 1 November 2026. The upcoming 2026 event is not reenacted.

00:00:00

From positions to policy

Welcome to Assembly. This animation uses fictional delegations to explain negotiation. It draws on the published Global Model WHO twenty twenty-five handbook. The twenty twenty-six Geneva event is scheduled for November ten to thirteen. This is a teaching reconstruction, not footage or a prediction of that event.

00:00:26

Open the agenda

The opening plenary establishes the agenda and organisation of work. Committee work includes an expert briefing. Delegates can question the evidence before examining a starting text, called a zero draft. In our fictional example, the question is how digital infrastructure can develop while protecting water and health services.

00:00:52

Understand the trade-off

Data centres use electricity. Some cooling systems consume water, and electricity generation can add indirect water demand. The footprint varies with location and technology. Our exercise asks delegates to negotiate safeguards. It does not assume that every data centre has the same impact, or that this is an official Geneva agenda item.

00:01:20

Make a concrete proposal

Aridia proposes: add protection for drinking water and essential health services during drought. Estara responds: we support safeguards, but cannot accept an undefined restriction on all digital services. Delegates identify the exact paragraph and explain both the requested change and its practical consequences.

00:01:46

Keep the disagreement visible

Unresolved wording can be bracketed and revisited. The facilitator asks which condition could resolve the objection. In this example, Aridia needs a credible drought trigger. Estara needs a predictable review process. The discussion shifts from opposing slogans to language both can implement.

00:02:10

Build a workable compromise

Kitala proposes a package: publish site-level water information, protect essential services during verified shortages, and phase in reporting with technical support. These are fictional teaching proposals. Delegates test the wording against their mandates. A paragraph agreed provisionally is marked agreed ad referendum, pending the complete outcome.

00:02:38

Check for remaining objections

The committee reviews the negotiated text and seeks adoption without a vote. Delegations may explain their positions. The committee outcome proceeds to plenary for final approval. Consensus does not mean everyone prefers every paragraph. An unresolved objection requires further work; an expiring classroom timer does not create agreement.

00:03:06

Turn agreement into action

Now apply the learning in your classroom. Record agreed wording and any unresolved differences. Assign implementation responsibilities, resources, a timetable and review indicators. Our teaching schedule provides ten minutes of prebrief, twenty of negotiation, fifteen for the report, and fifteen for debrief. These timings belong to Assembly, not the Geneva conference.

00:03:37

Learn from real negotiations

The real Intergovernmental Negotiating Body worked over several years on a pandemic instrument. Its process concluded with the Pandemic Agreement adopted in May twenty twenty-five. It is distinct from the student simulation. Explore the linked WHO sources, then enter solo practice or join your live classroom. The goal is reasoned compromise, not simply winning a debate.

Sources and scope

  • WHO INB: historical process
  • GMWHO 2025 handbook: simulation procedure, pp. 4–8
  • WFUNA: 2026 programme and dates
  • IEA: Energy and AI (2025), water and electricity context

The data-centre scenario and classroom timings are authored learning activities. They are not official WHO policy or the published 2026 conference agenda. Assembly follows a consensus-focused teaching pathway; this does not imply that all real WHO decisions are adopted without voting.
